name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - Sequence of steps in the Solvay process

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps involved in the manufacture of sodium carbonate by the Solvay process in the correct chronological sequence:

P. Precipitation of \(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3\) by reacting \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{HCO}_3\) with \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)
Q. Formation of \((\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{CO}_3\) by passing \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) into brine saturated with ammonia
R. Thermal decomposition of \(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3\) to yield \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\)
S. Conversion of \((\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{CO}_3\) into \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{HCO}_3\) with \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Solvay process converts sodium chloride into sodium carbonate by taking advantage of the low solubility of sodium hydrogencarbonate (\(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3\)) in aqueous solution.

Step 2: Chronological Reaction Sequence
First, \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) is passed into a concentrated \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) solution saturated with ammonia to form ammonium carbonate: \(2\mathrm{NH}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{CO}_2 \rightarrow (\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{CO}_3\) (step Q).
Second, ammonium carbonate reacts with more \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) to form ammonium hydrogencarbonate: \((\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{CO}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{CO}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{HCO}_3\) (step S).
Third, \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{HCO}_3\) reacts with \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) to precipitate sparingly soluble \(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3\): \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{HCO}_3 + \mathrm{NaCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl} + \mathrm{NaHCO}_3\) (step P).
Fourth, the separated \(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3\) crystals are heated to obtain sodium carbonate: \(2\mathrm{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3 + \mathrm{CO}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (step R).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence of steps is Q \(\rightarrow\) S \(\rightarrow\) P \(\rightarrow\) R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Sequence of steps to purify crude sodium chloride

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps for obtaining pure sodium chloride (\(\mathrm{NaCl}\)) from crude salt in the correct chronological sequence:

P. Saturating the filtered solution with hydrogen chloride (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) gas
Q. Dissolving the crude salt in the minimum amount of water
R. Separation of pure \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) crystals while more soluble \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) and \(\mathrm{MgCl}_2\) remain in solution
S. Filtering the solution to remove insoluble impurities

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Crude sodium chloride contains insoluble impurities as well as soluble deliquescent impurities such as \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) and \(\mathrm{MgCl}_2\). Pure \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is isolated by dissolution, filtration, and saturation with \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas.

Step 2: Chronological Process Sequence
First, the crude salt is dissolved in the minimum amount of water (step Q).
Second, the solution is filtered to remove insoluble impurities (step S).
Third, the clear solution is saturated with hydrogen chloride gas (step P).
Fourth, crystals of pure \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) separate out, while \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) and \(\mathrm{MgCl}_2\), being more soluble, remain in solution (step R).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is Q \(\rightarrow\) S \(\rightarrow\) P \(\rightarrow\) R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Sequence of steps in Castner-Kellner process

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events in the commercial manufacture of sodium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\)) by the Castner-Kellner cell in the correct sequence:

P. Treatment of sodium amalgam with water to produce \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), \(\mathrm{Hg}\), and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) gas
Q. Electrolysis of brine solution using a mercury cathode and a carbon anode
R. Combination of discharged sodium metal with mercury to form sodium amalgam
S. Discharge of \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) ions at the mercury cathode and evolution of \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) gas at the carbon anode

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sodium hydroxide is commercially prepared by electrolysing aqueous sodium chloride (brine) in a Castner-Kellner cell using a mercury cathode and a carbon anode.

Step 2: Chronological Process Sequence
First, brine solution is subjected to electrolysis in the Castner-Kellner cell using a mercury cathode and a carbon anode (step Q).
Second, during electrolysis, \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) ions are discharged at the cathode while \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) ions are oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) gas at the anode (step S).
Third, the sodium metal discharged at the cathode combines with mercury to form sodium amalgam (step R).
Fourth, the sodium amalgam is treated with water to yield sodium hydroxide, mercury, and hydrogen gas: \(2\mathrm{Na}\text{-amalgam} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH} + 2\mathrm{Hg} + \mathrm{H}_2\) (step P).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is Q \(\rightarrow\) S \(\rightarrow\) R \(\rightarrow\) P.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q04 - Thermal dehydration of washing soda to soda ash

questiontext.text:
When washing soda (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\cdot 10\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) is heated gradually and the final anhydrous product is subsequently dissolved in water, arrange the species formed in the correct chronological sequence:

P. Anhydrous sodium carbonate (soda ash), \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\)
Q. Alkaline solution containing \(\mathrm{HCO}_3^-\) and \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ions
R. Sodium carbonate monohydrate, \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\cdot \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)
S. Sodium carbonate decahydrate, \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\cdot 10\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrated sodium carbonate loses its water of crystallisation in stages upon heating, and the resulting carbonate ion undergoes hydrolysis in water.

Step 2: Chronological Sequence
Starting with sodium carbonate decahydrate, \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\cdot 10\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (S), heating converts it into sodium carbonate monohydrate, \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\cdot \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (R), with loss of \(9\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).
Heating above \(373\text{ K}\) removes the remaining water molecule to give anhydrous \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\), called soda ash (P).
Dissolving soda ash in water causes hydrolysis of the carbonate ion (\(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{HCO}_3^- + \mathrm{OH}^-\)), producing an alkaline solution containing \(\mathrm{HCO}_3^-\) and \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ions (Q).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is S \(\rightarrow\) R \(\rightarrow\) P \(\rightarrow\) Q.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q05 - Sequence of manufacture and setting of Portland cement

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following stages in the manufacture and setting of Portland cement in the correct chronological sequence:

P. Mixing the clinker with \(2\text{--}3\%\) by weight of gypsum (\(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\))
Q. Strongly heating a pulverised mixture of limestone and clay in a rotary kiln
R. Hydration of the constituent molecules and rearrangement to form a hard mass
S. Fusion and reaction of clay and lime to form cement clinker

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Portland cement is manufactured from limestone and clay, modified with gypsum to control its setting rate, and hardened by hydration upon mixing with water.

Step 2: Chronological Sequence
First, the raw materials, limestone and clay, are strongly heated together (step Q).
Second, clay and lime fuse and react to form 'cement clinker' (step S).
Third, this clinker is mixed with \(2\text{--}3\%\) by weight of gypsum (\(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) to form cement (step P).
Fourth, when mixed with water, setting occurs through hydration of the constituent molecules and their rearrangement to form a hard mass (step R).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is Q \(\rightarrow\) S \(\rightarrow\) P \(\rightarrow\) R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q06 - Sequence of reactions from limestone to calcium hydrogencarbonate

questiontext.text:
Starting from limestone (\(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\)), arrange the following transformations in the correct sequential order to obtain a clear solution of calcium hydrogencarbonate:

P. Passing limited \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) through lime water to form a milky suspension of \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\)
Q. Heating limestone at \(1070\text{--}1270\text{ K}\) to form quick lime (\(\mathrm{CaO}\))
R. Passing excess \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) to dissolve the precipitate as \(\mathrm{Ca(HCO}_3)_2\)
S. Slaking of quick lime with water to form \(\mathrm{Ca(OH)}_2\) (lime water)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Limestone undergoes thermal decomposition to quick lime, which slakes to calcium hydroxide; subsequent carbonation first precipitates insoluble calcium carbonate and then dissolves it as soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate.

Step 2: Chronological Reaction Sequence
First, heating limestone at \(1070\text{--}1270\text{ K}\) gives quick lime: \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO}_2\) (step Q).
Second, adding water to quick lime (slaking of lime) forms calcium hydroxide: \(\mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca(OH)}_2\) (step S).
Third, passing \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) through lime water turns it milky due to \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\) formation: \(\mathrm{Ca(OH)}_2 + \mathrm{CO}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCO}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (step P).
Fourth, passing excess \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) dissolves the precipitate to form soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate: \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3 + \mathrm{CO}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca(HCO}_3)_2\) (step R).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is Q \(\rightarrow\) S \(\rightarrow\) P \(\rightarrow\) R.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q07 - Decreasing order of reducing strength from standard potentials

questiontext.text: Given the standard electrode potentials (\(E^\circ\)): \(\mathrm{Cl}_2/\mathrm{Cl}^- = +1.36\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{I}_2/\mathrm{I}^- = +0.53\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Ag}^+/\mathrm{Ag} = +0.79\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Na}^+/\mathrm{Na} = -2.71\text{ V}\), and \(\mathrm{Li}^+/\mathrm{Li} = -3.04\text{ V}\). Arrange the species \(\mathrm{I}^-, \mathrm{Ag}, \mathrm{Cl}^-, \mathrm{Li}, \mathrm{Na}\) in decreasing order of reducing strength:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard reduction potentials: \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Li}^+/\mathrm{Li}) = -3.04\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Na}^+/\mathrm{Na}) = -2.71\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{I}_2/\mathrm{I}^-) = +0.53\text{ V}\), \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Ag}^+/\mathrm{Ag}) = +0.79\text{ V}\), and \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Cl}_2/\mathrm{Cl}^-) = +1.36\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Conceptual Principle
A more negative (or less positive) standard reduction potential \(E^\circ\) indicates a greater tendency for the reduced form of the couple to lose electrons and act as a stronger reducing agent.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Ordering
Ordering the \(E^\circ\) values from most negative to most positive gives:
\[-3.04\text{ V} < -2.71\text{ V} < +0.53\text{ V} < +0.79\text{ V} < +1.36\text{ V}\]
Therefore, the reducing strength of the corresponding reduced species decreases in the order:
\[\mathrm{Li} > \mathrm{Na} > \mathrm{I}^- > \mathrm{Ag} > \mathrm{Cl}^-\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct decreasing order of reducing strength is \(\mathrm{Li} > \mathrm{Na} > \mathrm{I}^- > \mathrm{Ag} > \mathrm{Cl}^-\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q08 - Increasing order of aqueous ionic mobilities of alkali metal ions

questiontext.text: Arrange the alkali metal ions \(\mathrm{Li}^+, \mathrm{Na}^+, \mathrm{K}^+, \mathrm{Rb}^+, \mathrm{Cs}^+\) in the correct increasing order of their ionic mobilities in aqueous solution:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In aqueous solution, cations are surrounded by water molecules (hydration). The smaller the bare ionic radius, the higher the charge density and the greater the degree of hydration, which increases the effective size (hydrated radius) of the moving ion.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Analysis
Hydration enthalpy and degree of hydration decrease down Group 1 in the order:
\[\mathrm{Li}^+ > \mathrm{Na}^+ > \mathrm{K}^+ > \mathrm{Rb}^+ > \mathrm{Cs}^+\]
Because \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) is the most heavily hydrated, it has the largest hydrated radius in water and therefore moves the slowest. Conversely, \(\mathrm{Cs}^+\) is the least hydrated, has the smallest hydrated radius, and moves the fastest.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of ionic mobilities in aqueous solution is \(\mathrm{Li}^+ < \mathrm{Na}^+ < \mathrm{K}^+ < \mathrm{Rb}^+ < \mathrm{Cs}^+\).
